Age: 29  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Persistent, excessive worry about work, finances, health, and children’s safety for 8 months, with associated restlessness, muscle tension, insomnia, irritability, and concentration difficulty; GAD‑7 score 16 (severe).  

Analysis: All three experts agreed that the presentation meets DSM‑5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) and that the case is non‑urgent, requiring outpatient management. Consensus identified the primary need for psychiatric involvement, either directly or in collaboration with primary care. Areas of divergence included: (1) the necessity of baseline laboratory studies—Expert B recommended routine CBC, CMP, and a urine drug screen, whereas Experts A and C considered them optional; (2) pharmacologic options—Expert B added SNRIs and buspirone as first‑line alternatives, while Experts A and C focused on SSRIs; (3) follow‑up timing—only Expert A specified a 2‑ to 4‑week interval for early reassessment. These differences are incorporated into the recommendations to ensure comprehensive care.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Review of existing thyroid function tests (normal); baseline complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel to establish a reference before initiating pharmacotherapy; urine drug screen if any substance use is suspected; urine pregnancy test for women of child‑bearing potential; PHQ‑9 for depressive symptoms; standardized substance‑use screening questionnaire; assessment of caffeine intake (including tea, energy drinks, supplements); review of over‑the‑counter and herbal products; family psychiatric history; evaluation of menstrual cycle, hormonal contraception, and other endocrine factors; formal suicide risk assessment.  

Conclusion: Diagnosis – Generalized Anxiety Disorder, moderate‑to‑severe; Management – non‑emergent outpatient care with psychiatric specialization.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  

Recommendations: Initiate evidence‑based treatment with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (e.g., sertraline 25 mg daily titrated as tolerated) as first‑line pharmacotherapy; consider a serotonin‑norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (e.g., venlafaxine) or buspirone if SSRIs are contraindicated or not tolerated, reflecting Expert B’s broader medication options. Refer promptly to a qualified therapist for cognitive‑behavioral therapy, and reinforce structured relaxation techniques, sleep‑hygiene counseling, regular aerobic exercise, and continued mindfulness practice. Conduct a comprehensive suicide risk assessment at the initial visit regardless of reported ideation. Screen for comorbid depression using PHQ‑9 and monitor for emergence of depressive symptoms. Obtain a urine pregnancy test before starting medication and discuss medication safety in pregnancy; if pregnant or planning pregnancy, consider non‑pharmacologic strategies first and involve obstetrics as needed. Document detailed caffeine consumption and advise limiting intake. Review all over‑the‑counter supplements and herbal remedies for potential interactions, especially with serotonergic agents. Collect a thorough family psychiatric history and assess social support, relationship stressors, and occupational pressures to tailor psychosocial interventions. Perform baseline CBC, CMP, and urine drug screen as recommended by Expert B, especially if any future substance use concerns arise. Schedule a follow‑up appointment in 2 to 4 weeks to evaluate medication tolerability, symptom response, side‑effects, and any new safety concerns; thereafter, arrange monthly visits until stable, then quarterly maintenance reviews. Adjust medication dose or switch agents based on response and side‑effect profile, and continue psychotherapy throughout.  

Notes: The patient has already attempted meditation and regular exercise with partial benefit; these should be continued as adjuncts to the formal treatment plan.

Complaint: Persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea for 2 years; symptoms year‑round and worsen with dusting/vacuuming.

Analysis: The clinical picture (bilateral pale, boggy mucosa, transverse nasal crease, clear rhinorrhea, dust‑mite trigger) aligns with perennial allergic rhinitis. All three experts concur on this primary diagnosis and on the non‑emergent nature of the condition, as well as on Otolaryngology (ENT) being the appropriate sub‑specialty. Expert B emphasized a broad differential (non‑allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, structural abnormalities, polyposis, infectious rhinitis) and listed specific red‑flag findings that would mandate urgent evaluation. Expert C listed a shorter differential (non‑allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, polyposis, structural issues) and highlighted environmental control as a central intervention. Expert A did not provide a classification, indicating lower confidence. Consensus differed on the necessity of nasal cytology (mentioned only by Expert B) and on the early inclusion of a leukotriene receptor antagonist (suggested by Expert B but not by Expert C). Both experts agree that diagnosis is primarily clinical, with allergen testing reserved for unclear cases or before immunotherapy.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Nasal endoscopy (if atypical findings develop), skin prick testing or serum‑specific IgE for dust‑mite and other indoor aeroallergens, optional nasal cytology for eosinophils, sinus CT scan only if chronic sinusitis or structural abnormality is suspected, routine otolaryngologic examination.

Conclusion: Perennial allergic rhinitis, likely driven by dust‑mite sensitization.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Initiate intranasal corticosteroid spray daily and saline nasal irrigation to address congestion and mucosal inflammation. Add a second‑generation oral antihistamine taken daily for sneezing and rhinorrhea. Advise strict environmental control: encase mattress and pillows in allergen‑proof covers, replace carpeted bedrooms with hard flooring where feasible, maintain indoor humidity below 50 %, use a HEPA‑filter vacuum, and ensure adequate ventilation to reduce mold spores. Because intermittent over‑the‑counter antihistamine use suggests suboptimal adherence, provide counseling on daily medication use and set up a medication reminder system. Consider adding a leukotriene receptor antagonist if symptoms remain moderate‑to‑severe after 4–6 weeks of combined intranasal steroid and antihistamine therapy. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 4–6 weeks to assess symptom control; if control is inadequate, arrange allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE) and discuss allergen‑specific immunotherapy. Monitor for development of asthma or aspirin‑exacerbated respiratory disease, especially if new lower‑airway symptoms appear. Counsel the patient to avoid topical nasal decongestants to prevent rhinitis medicamentosa. If red‑flag signs emerge (unilateral obstruction, purulent or bloody discharge, facial pain/pressure, fever, anosmia, visual changes, epistaxis, or nasal mass), advise immediate ENT or emergency evaluation. Optional nasal cytology can be performed if the clinical picture is atypical or if there is uncertainty about eosinophilic inflammation.

Notes: The chronic nature of symptoms may impair sleep quality, daily productivity, and overall quality of life; address these impacts during follow‑up. Family history of atopy, though not reported, should be queried as it may influence disease severity and management decisions. Consider evaluation for comorbid sinusitis or adenoid hypertrophy if symptoms persist despite optimal therapy.

Age: 16 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Fever, sore throat, fatigue, difficulty swallowing, cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis with soft‑palate petechiae, faint macular rash on trunk and arms  

Analysis: The panel converged on primary Epstein‑Barr virus infectious mononucleosis as the most likely diagnosis, based on the classic triad of fever, exudative pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy together with soft‑palate petechiae, rash and marked fatigue in an adolescent. All three experts agreed on a non‑emergent outpatient pathway, on pediatric primary‑care as the initial managing specialty, and on a largely supportive diagnostic and therapeutic approach. Points of divergence included the exact timing of the first follow‑up (Expert A and B favored 48‑72 hours, Expert C initially suggested 24‑48 hours but later aligned with a 48‑72 hour window) and the conditional use of corticosteroids (all agreed steroids are reserved for imminent airway obstruction, but Expert C emphasized a more aggressive stance on early consideration). The outlier view that the case required emergent care was rejected after consensus that no objective airway or severe dehydration signs were present.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CBC with differential, heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, throat culture or rapid streptococcal antigen test, EBV‑specific serology if Monospot negative, liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin), C‑reactive protein or ESR, HIV test if risk factors present, CMV serology if indicated, pregnancy test, bedside assessment of hydration (mucous membranes, capillary refill, skin turgor, urine output), orthostatic vital signs if needed, focused abdominal exam for splenomegaly, neck examination for peritonsillar abscess, ultrasound of the neck or abdomen only if clinical suspicion for abscess or splenomegaly, immunization record review.  

Conclusion: Infectious mononucleosis due to primary EBV infection is the leading diagnosis; alternative etiologies such as streptococcal pharyngitis, CMV, acute HIV seroconversion, viral hepatitis, peritonsillar abscess, and other listed differentials should be ruled out as indicated.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Arrange same‑day or next‑day outpatient evaluation by a pediatric primary‑care clinician. Obtain the laboratory panel listed above, including a pregnancy test given the patient’s age and potential medication implications. Perform a thorough physical exam for splenomegaly; if the spleen is enlarged, counsel strict avoidance of contact sports and heavy exertion for at least 4 weeks and repeat imaging if size is uncertain. Assess hydration status clinically and initiate oral fluids; consider IV fluids only if oral intake is insufficient. Evaluate for peritonsillar abscess by inspecting for unilateral severe pain, trismus, uvular deviation or muffled voice; if present, obtain neck ultrasound or contrast‑enhanced CT and involve ENT promptly. Obtain a sexual history and assess HIV risk; order HIV testing when indicated. Review vaccination history (MMR, varicella, influenza, COVID‑19) to exclude vaccine‑preventable exanthems and document for future care. Ask about recent travel or sick contacts to broaden the differential. Avoid prescribing ampicillin‑class antibiotics to prevent the characteristic maculopapular rash; treat confirmed streptococcal co‑infection with appropriate penicillin or alternative. Use NSAIDs cautiously, recognizing rare reports of rash exacerbation in EBV. Counsel the patient and family about the expected disease course, the possibility of prolonged fatigue lasting weeks to months, and signs of chronic fatigue syndrome. Provide mental‑health screening using PHQ‑9 and GAD‑7; refer for further evaluation if positive. Schedule a follow‑up visit in 48‑72 hours with explicit red‑flag criteria: worsening dysphagia, drooling, stridor, new or enlarging neck mass, persistent high‑grade fever beyond 7 days, abdominal pain suggestive of splenic involvement, signs of dehydration, or any respiratory distress. Instruct the patient to return immediately for any of these symptoms. If airway compromise or severe tonsillar hypertrophy develops, initiate short‑course corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 3–5 days) after discussing risks and benefits, and arrange ENT evaluation. Monitor liver function tests; if transaminases rise markedly or jaundice appears, consider hepatology referral.  

Notes: Ensure documentation of all assessments, counseling points, and follow‑up plans in the medical record.

Age: 4 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Rapidly progressive sore throat, dysphagia, noisy breathing, drooling, fever, and audible inspiratory stridor  

Analysis: The child presents with classic signs of acute epiglottitis—tripod positioning, profuse drooling, muffled voice, stridor, tachypnea, tachycardia, high fever, hypoxia, and refusal to swallow—combined with a lateral neck X‑ray showing the thumb sign. All three experts agreed on the diagnosis of acute epiglottitis and on the life‑threatening nature of the airway obstruction, requiring immediate multidisciplinary involvement (Anesthesiology, ENT, Emergency Medicine). Consensus also existed on pre‑airway measures (upright positioning, supplemental oxygen, careful IV access, fluid resuscitation, antipyretics, empiric third‑generation cephalosporin) and on definitive airway management via rapid‑sequence intubation with surgical airway backup. The only point of divergence was Expert B’s suggestion that flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy could be performed if the airway appeared stable; Experts A and C, supported by the majority, rejected any endoscopic examination before securing the airway due to the high risk of precipitating complete obstruction. The panel also noted that while the thumb sign is specific, it is not 100 % sensitive, and clinical judgment must prevail if imaging and exam are discordant.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Lateral neck X‑ray (thumb sign), complete blood count, blood cultures, basic metabolic panel, large‑bore intravenous access, supplemental oxygen delivery system, rapid‑sequence intubation equipment, surgical airway kit (cricothyrotomy/tracheostomy set), intravenous ceftriaxone (or equivalent third‑generation cephalosporin), optional dexamethasone, vaccination record review  

Conclusion: Acute epiglottitis in an incompletely immunized 4‑year‑old boy with imminent airway compromise; emergent airway protection is mandatory.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Keep the child upright and calm; provide supplemental oxygen by non‑threatening method (e.g., blow‑by); obtain large‑bore IV access with minimal agitation; begin isotonic fluid bolus to address possible sepsis; administer antipyretics; start empiric IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) promptly; defer any oral, pharyngeal, or endoscopic examination until after the airway is secured; activate the multidisciplinary team (Anesthesiology, ENT, Emergency Medicine) without delay; proceed to rapid‑sequence intubation in a controlled environment with immediate availability of surgical airway equipment; after successful intubation, consider a short course of IV dexamethasone if airway edema is significant and it will not delay care; obtain blood cultures and CBC after airway control; continue IV antibiotics for 7‑10 days; admit to pediatric ICU for continuous airway and hemodynamic monitoring; reassess for re‑obstruction and plan for safe extubation; update the child’s immunizations, completing the Hib series; report the Hib infection to public‑health authorities; provide thorough family counseling regarding disease severity, ICU stay, vaccination importance, and signs of recurrence.  

Notes: Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy should only be performed after the airway is definitively secured, if additional anatomic detail is required; the thumb sign, while specific, does not replace clinical assessment; maintain readiness for emergent surgical airway throughout the procedure.

Sex: Male  
Complaint: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, insomnia with early‑morning awakening, significant weight loss (14 lb), psychomotor retardation, poor grooming, feelings of worthlessness, and impaired concentration for 2 months following a relationship breakup.  

Analysis: All three experts converged on a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, severe, without psychotic features, supported by DSM‑5 criteria and a PHQ‑9 score of 22. Consensus also agreed that the case does not constitute an immediate psychiatric emergency but requires prompt, intensive outpatient management by psychiatry. The experts uniformly identified the need for a comprehensive medical work‑up to exclude organic contributors given the marked weight loss and psychomotor slowing. Points of divergence included the breadth of differential diagnoses (Expert A emphasized adjustment disorder, bipolar depression, substance‑induced mood disorder, and medical conditions; Expert B added dysthymia and medication side effects; Expert C highlighted Persistent Complex Bereavement Disorder and the possibility of malignancy). Red‑flag considerations also varied: Expert A mentioned catatonia as a potential concern, whereas Experts B and C did not. Recommended psychotherapy differed (CBT versus interpersonal therapy focused on role transition). Follow‑up intervals ranged from a single 1‑2 week visit (Expert A) to weekly visits for the first month (Expert C) and a combined schedule of 1‑2 weeks then repeat PHQ‑9 in 2‑4 weeks (Expert B). Laboratory panels were largely consistent (CBC, CMP, thyroid studies, B12/folate) with Expert B additionally suggesting a urine drug screen and HIV/syphilis serology.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid‑stimulating hormone with free T4, serum vitamin B12 and folate levels, urinalysis, urine toxicology screen, and, if clinically indicated, HIV and syphilis serology.  

Conclusion: Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, severe, without psychotic features.  

Emergency type: Requires non‑emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  

Recommendations: Initiate first‑line antidepressant therapy with an SSRI (e.g., sertraline or escitalopram) while providing detailed psychoeducation about medication expectations, side‑effects, and the need for close monitoring of emergent suicidality, especially during the first weeks of treatment. Refer for psychotherapy promptly; given the recent breakup, interpersonal therapy targeting role transition and grief is preferred, but cognitive‑behavioral therapy remains an acceptable alternative. Develop a written safety plan and ensure the patient has 24‑hour crisis contact information. Schedule an initial follow‑up appointment within 1 to 2 weeks to assess medication tolerance, re‑evaluate suicidal ideation, and review laboratory results. Continue weekly visits for the first month, then transition to bi‑weekly or monthly visits based on clinical response, with repeat PHQ‑9 scoring at 2‑4 weeks to gauge improvement. Conduct a thorough medical history focusing on family history of mood or bipolar disorders, current or recent substance use, medication side‑effects, and any prior endocrine or hematologic conditions. Document baseline functional status at work and home, assess social support networks, living situation, and caregiver involvement to inform treatment planning. Re‑assess for possible bipolar spectrum features if any mood elevation emerges, and remain vigilant for catatonic signs despite their low probability. If laboratory work‑up reveals abnormalities (e.g., thyroid dysfunction, anemia, vitamin deficiencies, or positive toxicology), treat the medical condition concurrently and adjust the psychiatric management plan accordingly.  

Notes: The significant unintentional weight loss and psychomotor retardation warrant prompt exclusion of serious medical illness (e.g., malignancy, endocrine disorder, infection). Ongoing evaluation of psychosocial stressors and support systems is essential for sustained recovery.

Expert B highlighted peri‑operative cardiac risk assessment, tight glycemic control, DVT prophylaxis, and medication review, while Expert A focused on standard pre‑operative labs and Expert C on the need for prompt antibiotics and surgery. These differences are incorporated into the recommendations to ensure a comprehensive approach.

Obtain the laboratory panel outlined above to assess baseline status, guide fluid and antibiotic management, and evaluate cardiac risk. Perform a focused cardiac assessment, including ECG and, if clinically indicated, echocardiography, given the history of coronary artery disease. Optimize glycemic control with insulin infusion as needed. Review antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications in light of recent knee replacement and plan peri‑operative DVT prophylaxis (mechanical compression and pharmacologic prophylaxis when bleeding risk permits). Provide analgesia as required, avoiding NSAIDs that may impair renal function or platelet aggregation. Arrange urgent surgical consultation with General Surgery for appendectomy, preferably laparoscopic if the operative field permits; be prepared for conversion to open if intra‑abdominal contamination is encountered. Post‑operatively, monitor for signs of peritonitis, intra‑abdominal abscess, sepsis, wound infection, and cardiac complications. Continue DVT prophylaxis, maintain tight glucose control, and reassess cardiac status daily until stable.

Sex: Male  
Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and mild headache that worsen with prolonged computer screen use; symptoms improve on weekends.  

Analysis: All three experts converged on the diagnosis of computer vision syndrome (digital eye strain) as the most likely explanation for the patient’s symptoms, given the temporal relationship to screen time, normal visual acuity, and lack of red‑flag findings. Consensus was also reached that the condition is non‑urgent and self‑care appropriate, and that ophthalmology (or optometry) is the appropriate subclinical specialty for initial evaluation. Areas of minor disagreement involved the breadth of the differential diagnosis and the need for ancillary testing. Expert A emphasized that no immediate diagnostic tests are required, whereas Expert B suggested a basic refraction and dry‑eye assessment if symptoms persist, and Expert C highlighted the possibility of subtle refractive or binocular vision abnormalities that might warrant near‑point convergence testing. Expert B additionally recommended a routine follow‑up in 2–4 weeks, a point not explicitly stated by the other two experts. These nuances are incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: At this visit no specific tests are mandatory; a standard visual acuity chart and slit‑lamp examination have already been performed. If symptoms do not improve with initial self‑care measures, consider: autorefractor or trial lenses for refraction, tear‑film break‑up time or Schirmer strip for dry‑eye assessment, and a near‑point of convergence ruler or binocular vision testing equipment.  

Conclusion: The presentation is consistent with computer vision syndrome (digital eye strain) secondary to prolonged screen use; the condition is self‑care appropriate and does not require emergent intervention.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  

Recommendations: Implement the 20‑20‑20 rule (every 20 minutes look at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and take a 5‑minute break from the screen at least once per hour; adjust workstation ergonomics by positioning the monitor at eye level, maintaining a viewing distance of about 50–70 cm, reducing glare with appropriate lighting, and using a matte screen filter if needed; use preservative‑free artificial tears several times daily to alleviate dryness and stay well hydrated; perform a brief ocular surface assessment and consider tear‑film break‑up time or Schirmer testing only if dryness persists despite lubricants; obtain a basic refraction to rule out subtle uncorrected refractive error and, if near‑point convergence is abnormal, refer for binocular vision evaluation; review current medications for anticholinergic properties that may exacerbate dry eye; arrange a workplace ergonomic assessment to identify posture, lighting, or glare issues; counsel the patient that blue‑light filtering glasses have limited evidence and should not replace ergonomic measures; schedule a follow‑up ophthalmology visit in 2–4 weeks to reassess symptoms, ensure improvement, and decide whether further testing (e.g., detailed dry‑eye work‑up or binocular vision testing) is warranted; if new symptoms such as sudden visual loss, photophobia, eye pain, or visual field changes develop, seek prompt evaluation.  

Notes: Emphasize that systemic causes of dry eye, such as autoimmune disease, are only considered if ocular symptoms worsen or fail to respond to the above measures.

Complaint: Shortness of breath and cough of several days’ duration with recent increase in white sputum production; chronic morning productive cough for years.  

Analysis: The panel unanimously identified an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (COPD flare) as the most likely diagnosis, based on the patient’s 40‑year smoking history, longstanding productive cough, and recent worsening after an upper‑respiratory viral prodrome. All experts agreed that no red‑flag symptoms (hemoptysis, fever, weight loss, severe dyspnea at rest) are present, supporting non‑emergent outpatient management. Consensus also placed pulmonology as the appropriate specialty for further evaluation. Points of divergence included antibiotic use and advanced imaging: Expert B recommended against antibiotics and advised chest CT only if the chest X‑ray is abnormal, whereas Expert C allowed conditional oral antibiotics if sputum becomes purulent and advocated proactive low‑dose CT screening for lung cancer once COPD is confirmed. Both perspectives were incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest radiograph (to exclude pneumonia or mass); baseline spirometry (to confirm airflow limitation and stage COPD); pulse oximetry and measurement of vital signs (including oxygen saturation); COVID‑19 test (given recent rhinorrhea); assessment of vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal); if chest X‑ray abnormal or symptoms persist, consider sputum culture, CBC, and low‑dose CT chest for lung‑cancer screening (per high‑risk criteria).  

Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (COPD flare) in a long‑term smoker, requiring outpatient evaluation and pulmonology follow‑up.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations: Initiate short‑acting bronchodilator therapy (e.g., albuterol inhaler) and advise adequate hydration; provide intensive smoking‑cessation counseling with offer of pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion). Verify and update influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations. Perform COVID‑19 testing to rule out viral infection. Obtain chest X‑ray and spirometry at the initial visit; record pulse oximetry and full vital signs to stratify risk. If sputum becomes purulent or clinical deterioration occurs, consider a short course of oral antibiotics. Schedule follow‑up in 1–2 weeks; if symptoms persist, obtain sputum culture, CBC, and arrange full pulmonary function testing. Should the chest X‑ray reveal abnormalities or if COPD is confirmed, arrange low‑dose CT screening for lung cancer in accordance with guidelines for high‑risk smokers. Explore occupational or indoor pollutant exposures, family history of lung disease, and prior exacerbations or hospitalizations to refine risk assessment. Consider testing for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency only if COPD is diagnosed at a younger age or there is a suggestive family history.  

Notes: Ensure patient education on recognizing red‑flag symptoms (new hemoptysis, fever, worsening dyspnea) that would necessitate urgent reassessment.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Evaluate for immunocompromise (e.g., HIV status, chronic steroid use) and ask about pregnancy; avoid medications contraindicated in pregnancy. Review recent travel history and contact with individuals known to have influenza or other transmissible infections. If chronic rhinitis is identified, discuss the potential role of intranasal corticosteroids or antihistamine sprays after the acute episode resolves.  

Notes: The patient’s presentation aligns with typical viral URI patterns; no further work‑up is indicated at this time.

Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy red papules on forearms and lower legs that appeared over the past 24 hours after outdoor play.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnosed papular urticaria (insect‑bite hypersensitivity reaction) based on the acute onset of pruritic erythematous papules with central puncta on exposed extremities, absence of systemic symptoms, and lack of signs of infection or other dermatoses. Consensus was reached on the non‑urgent nature of the condition, the appropriateness of primary‑care pediatric management, and the core differential list (contact dermatitis, scabies, viral exanthem, urticaria, early bacterial infection, and early Lyme disease in endemic areas). The only minor variation among experts was the emphasis on early Lyme disease as a possible, but unlikely, consideration; no expert required routine testing for it. No outlier positions were identified.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for this classic presentation. Reserve skin scraping, complete blood count, or Lyme serology only if atypical features, red‑flag signs, or epidemiologic exposure to ticks emerge.  

Conclusion: Papular urticaria (insect‑bite hypersensitivity reaction).  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Provide topical antipruritic therapy (calamine lotion or low‑potency hydrocortisone 1 %) and an oral second‑generation antihistamine to control itching. Advise caregivers to keep the child’s nails trimmed and to discourage scratching to reduce the risk of secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization). Instruct to monitor for red‑flag signs such as fever, rapidly spreading erythema, purulent drainage, lymphangitis, angioedema, respiratory distress, systemic malaise, arthralgia, or neurologic changes; seek medical care promptly if any develop. Educate on insect‑bite prevention: use age‑appropriate repellents, dress the child in protective clothing, and reduce standing water or other breeding sites in the yard. Assess for recent pet exposure or pest infestations and discuss environmental measures (e.g., lawn mowing timing, insect control). Review the child’s atopic history and prior similar episodes to gauge susceptibility and response to past treatments. Verify tetanus immunization status in case of skin breaks from scratching. If the child resides in or has visited a Lyme‑endemic area and a tick bite is suspected, consider early Lyme disease and obtain serology only if an erythema migrans‑like lesion or other suggestive signs appear. Schedule routine follow‑up in 3–5 days to ensure lesion resolution; earlier evaluation if worsening or red‑flag signs occur.  

Notes: The central puncta strongly support arthropod bites; scabies is unlikely given the absence of burrows or interdigital lesions. The condition is self‑limited and responds well to symptomatic care.

A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.

Age: 24 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Dysuria, urinary frequency, progressive right flank pain, fever, rigors, nausea and one episode of vomiting  

Analysis: All three experts diagnosed acute pyelonephritis and agreed that the patient meets criteria for emergent care because she exhibits high‑grade fever, tachycardia, borderline hypotension, rigors, vomiting and systemic inflammatory response syndrome, all of which raise concern for early sepsis. Consensus also identified the Emergency Department as the appropriate initial point of care, the need for immediate fluid resuscitation, empiric broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and collection of urine and blood cultures. Red‑flag features (temperature > 102 °F, rigors, tachycardia, borderline hypotension, CVA tenderness, vomiting) were uniformly highlighted. Laboratory work‑up (CBC, BMP, serum lactate, cultures) was agreed upon. Where the panel diverged was the timing of renal imaging: Experts A and B recommended imaging only if clinical suspicion for obstruction, abscess, or stone exists or if the patient fails to improve within 48–72 hours, whereas Expert C, after reconsideration, advocated for early imaging (ultrasound first) given the severity of illness, vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake. This difference is noted and incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urinalysis, urine culture, blood cultures, complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel (electrolytes, creatinine), serum lactate, electrocardiogram (baseline), bedside cardiac and respiratory monitoring, intravenous access, intravenous crystalloid fluids, and renal imaging (renal ultrasound as first‑line, CT abdomen/pelvis if ultrasound inconclusive or high suspicion for obstruction/abscess).  

Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis with systemic inflammatory response/sepsis requiring emergent emergency‑department evaluation and inpatient admission.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  

Recommendations: Initiate sepsis‑bundle care in the Emergency Department – obtain two large‑bore IV lines, administer a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus (adjust for cardiac status), and draw blood for CBC, BMP, lactate, and cultures before antibiotics. Obtain urine sample for culture and urinalysis. Start empiric intravenous broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering common uropathogens and resistant strains (e.g., ceftriaxone 1–2 g q24 h; consider cefepime or a carbapenem if ESBL risk, or IV fluoroquinolone if local susceptibility and no contraindication). Record a detailed drug‑allergy history and review recent antibiotic exposure to guide selection. Provide antipyretics, analgesia, and antiemetics as needed. Monitor vital signs, urine output, and repeat lactate after fluid resuscitation; treat any lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L as evidence of sepsis. Assess hydration status clinically (skin turgor, mucous membranes, urine output) and correct deficits aggressively. Implement venous thromboembolism prophylaxis (e.g., low‑dose low‑molecular‑weight heparin) if the patient will be immobilized.  

Imaging: Perform a bedside renal ultrasound promptly to evaluate for obstruction, hydronephrosis, or abscess given the patient’s vomiting, inability to maintain oral intake, and systemic severity. If ultrasound is nondiagnostic or high suspicion persists, obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen/pelvis. If no imaging indication is present and the patient stabilizes, defer imaging for 48–72 hours and repeat if clinical improvement is not observed.  

Admission: Admit to an inpatient unit with capability for sepsis monitoring (step‑down or ICU if hemodynamic instability worsens). Continue intravenous antibiotics, fluid management, and serial lactate measurements. Transition to oral antibiotics when afebrile, tolerating oral intake, and cultures allow de‑escalation, completing a total 10–14‑day course.  

Follow‑up: Arrange outpatient follow‑up with primary care or urology within 1–2 weeks after discharge. Review culture results, adjust antibiotics if needed, and assess for resolution of symptoms. Because of two prior UTIs in the past year, evaluate for anatomic or functional abnormalities after the acute episode (renal/bladder ultrasound; consider voiding cystourethrogram if indicated). Counsel on adequate hydration, proper voiding habits, and strategies to reduce recurrence. Discuss the potential need for prophylactic antibiotics only after documented recurrent infections despite correction of predisposing factors.  

Notes: The patient is immunocompetent based on history; however, screen for diabetes or other immunosuppressive conditions if clinical suspicion arises. Negative pregnancy test eliminates obstetric causes, but maintain awareness of rare ectopic pregnancy in differential if pelvic pain evolves. Suprapubic tenderness may reflect concurrent cystitis; ensure treatment covers lower urinary tract infection as well.

The key elements supporting this diagnosis are unilateral dermatomal pain preceding a vesicular rash, the evolution of lesions through pustulation to crusting, systemic symptoms, and the patient’s advanced age, which predisposes to varicella‑zoster virus reactivation. Consensus was reached on the diagnosis, on the emergency classification (“Requires non-emergent care”), and on a high level of confidence (95 % for Experts A and C, 90 % for Expert B). Divergence occurred only in the subclinical specialty: Experts A and C voted for Infectious Disease, while Expert B favored Dermatology. The final consensus label is Infectious Disease. A secondary disagreement was noted in round 2 regarding the adequacy of the questionnaire; however, in the final round all experts agreed that the vignette provided sufficient information to answer the diagnostic question. An outlier confidence rating of 0 % from Expert A was identified and deemed inconsistent with the strong clinical evidence.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Clinical examination (inspection of rash distribution and lesion morphology); Tzanck smear or PCR of vesicle fluid for varicella‑zoster virus if diagnostic uncertainty exists; basic laboratory tests (CBC, renal function) to assess suitability for antiviral therapy; pain assessment scale.
Conclusion: Herpes zoster (shingles) affecting a thoracic dermatome.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Initiate oral antiviral therapy (e.g., valacyclovir 1 g three times daily) as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, to reduce viral replication and complications. Provide analgesia tailored to pain severity, including NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or neuropathic agents (gabapentin or pregabalin) if needed. Counsel the patient on the risk of post‑herpetic neuralgia and arrange follow‑up within 1 week to assess response and side‑effects. Although the consensus subclinical specialty is Infectious Disease, collaboration with Dermatology is advisable for skin‑specific management and for patients with atypical presentations. The questionnaire is deemed sufficient; no additional items are required for diagnosis. The low confidence rating reported by Expert A should be considered an outlier and does not alter the management plan.
Notes: Monitor renal function before and during antiviral therapy, especially in elderly patients. Consider vaccination with recombinant zoster vaccine for future prevention if the patient has not been immunized. Document lesion progression and pain scores to evaluate for post‑herpetic neuralgia.

EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. Age: 28 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Continuous generalized tonic‑clonic seizure activity lasting >12 minutes despite pre‑hospital and emergency department benzodiazepines  

Analysis: The panel unanimously identifies refractory convulsive status epilepticus (RSE) as the primary diagnosis, defined by ongoing seizures after two adequate benzodiazepine doses (IM midazolam 10 mg and IV lorazepam 4 mg). All experts agree that RSE is a life‑threatening emergency requiring immediate airway protection, rapid seizure termination, and ICU admission. Consensus also highlights red‑flag features—prolonged seizure duration, benzodiazepine failure, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, hypoxia, cyanosis, irregular respirations, and recent antiepileptic drug non‑adherence—that increase morbidity and mortality.  

Differences emerged regarding the immediate diagnostic work‑up and the leading specialty. Experts A and B did not initially emphasize a pregnancy test, whereas Expert C added eclampsia to the differential and advocated for immediate pregnancy testing, prompting the panel to adopt this recommendation. Likewise, while Expert C suggested emergency‑medicine‑led resuscitation with neurology consultation, the extra considerations note that neurology should be the primary lead for ongoing seizure management and EEG interpretation, with emergency medicine directing initial resuscitation. These outlier‑driven adjustments have been incorporated into the final protocol.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Point‑of‑care glucose meter; rapid‑turnaround laboratory panel including CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, renal and hepatic function, creatine kinase, lactate, arterial blood gas, toxicology screen, antiepileptic drug level, blood cultures; serum β‑hCG (pregnancy test); non‑contrast head CT; emergent EEG after airway control; lumbar puncture after CT if no contraindications; continuous capnography; cardiac telemetry; invasive blood pressure monitoring; temperature monitoring and active cooling devices.  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing refractory convulsive status epilepticus with respiratory and hemodynamic compromise, necessitating emergent airway management, second‑line antiseizure therapy, and admission to an ICU or neurocritical care unit for continuous EEG‑guided anesthetic coma and multidisciplinary support.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  

Recommendations: Secure the airway immediately with rapid‑sequence endotracheal intubation, initiate mechanical ventilation with 100 % oxygen, and employ continuous capnography to verify ventilation. Begin active cooling measures to lower core temperature from 39.2 °C, using external cooling blankets or evaporative techniques while monitoring for shivering. Administer a second‑line intravenous antiseizure medication without delay—options include fosphenytoin, levetiracetam (dose adjusted for renal function), valproate, or phenobarbital—selected based on patient comorbidities and institutional protocol. If seizures persist, commence a continuous anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital) in the ICU, titrating to electrographic seizure cessation under continuous EEG monitoring. Obtain the full laboratory panel outlined above, including serum β‑hCG, to evaluate for eclampsia; a positive pregnancy test mandates magnesium sulfate therapy, avoidance of teratogenic agents such as valproate, and obstetric consultation. Assess renal function (serum creatinine, eGFR) before dosing levetiracetam or other renally cleared agents, adjusting loading and maintenance doses accordingly. Perform non‑contrast head CT promptly; if imaging is negative for mass effect, proceed with lumbar puncture after ensuring coagulation status is adequate, to rule out CNS infection. Initiate broad‑spectrum antibiotics and antivirals empirically if infection is suspected, guided by culture results. Monitor cardiac rhythm continuously, treat severe hypertension per protocol, and obtain serial CK, electrolytes, and lactate to detect rhabdomyolysis, metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte disturbances. Engage social work early to address insurance barriers, facilitate medication access, and arrange outpatient follow‑up to improve adherence. Maintain multidisciplinary coordination among emergency medicine, neurology, critical care, pharmacy, obstetrics (if pregnant), and social services throughout the hospitalization.  

Notes: The presence of cyanosis, irregular respirations, and hypoxia underscores the urgency of airway protection. Hyperthermia may be ictal or infectious; active cooling and infection work‑up are both essential. Propofol infusion syndrome risk should be mitigated by limiting dose and duration, with vigilant monitoring for metabolic derangements.

Age: 31 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Six‑month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge, amenorrhea for 6 months, progressive headaches, weight gain, lethargy, decreased libido, and infertility.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified a prolactin‑secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma) as the most likely diagnosis, based on markedly elevated serum prolactin (500 µg/L), galactorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, infertility, and a sellar mass measuring approximately 1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm on MRI. Consensus also agreed that the case requires non‑emergent but prompt care and that management falls under Endocrinology. Points of divergence included: (1) the emphasis on ruling out macroprolactin interference, (2) the extent of baseline hormonal testing (full pituitary panel versus selective tests), (3) the timing of formal visual‑field testing (immediate versus contingent on symptom change), (4) the inclusion of surgical and radiotherapy options as secondary strategies, and (5) the identification of specific red‑flag findings that would convert care to emergent. These differences are incorporated into the recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the brain with contrast (already obtained), serum prolactin repeat with macroprolactin assay, comprehensive pituitary hormone panel (ACTH, cortisol, LH, FSH, estradiol, GH, IGF‑1, TSH, free T4), visual‑field testing (automated perimetry), basic metabolic panel, renal and hepatic function tests, pregnancy test, ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram if cabergoline is continued long‑term, PHQ‑9 depression screen, and medication review for prolactin‑raising agents.  

Conclusion: The patient has a macroprolactinoma presenting with hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, hypogonadotropic amenorrhea, and headaches, without visual‑field deficits or signs of pituitary apoplexy.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate dopamine‑agonist therapy, preferably cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly, with dose titration based on prolactin response and tolerability; if cabergoline is contraindicated, use bromocriptine. Obtain a repeat prolactin level with macroprolactin assay within 1 week to confirm true hyperprolactinemia. Perform a full pituitary hormone assessment and baseline morning cortisol and ACTH before starting therapy; replace adrenal insufficiency if identified. Conduct automated visual‑field testing now to establish a baseline and repeat if symptoms evolve. Review all current medications for potential prolactin‑raising effects, although none are apparent. Order a transthoracic echocardiogram before initiating long‑term cabergoline and repeat annually if therapy exceeds 2 years, given the rare risk of valvular disease. Screen for depression with PHQ‑9 and arrange counseling or psychotherapy as needed. Evaluate thyroid function beyond TSH by measuring free T4 to exclude subtle hypothyroidism contributing to weight gain and lethargy. Counsel the patient on the risks of NSAID overuse and consider a referral to a headache specialist if headaches persist after prolactin normalization. Provide education on signs of pituitary apoplexy (sudden severe headache, visual changes, altered consciousness) and instruct her to seek immediate medical attention if they occur. Schedule follow‑up prolactin measurement at 4–6 weeks, repeat MRI at 6–12 months, and reassess visual fields at each follow‑up visit or sooner if visual symptoms develop. Discuss fertility planning, including timing of ovulation monitoring once prolactin normalizes, and offer referral to reproductive endocrinology if conception does not occur within 6–12 months.  

Notes: The patient’s family history does not suggest a hereditary pituitary syndrome; genetic testing is not indicated at this time.

Age: 44 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain with lethargy and refractory hypotension after viral gastroenteritis; unable to retain oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.  

Analysis: The panel unanimously identified an acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by loss of oral glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement during gastroenteritis. All experts agreed on the life‑threatening complications—refractory hypotension, severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, profound hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, and altered mental status—and on the need for immediate ICU‑level resuscitation. Consensus was reached that Emergency Medicine should lead the initial stabilization while Endocrinology provides definitive hormone management; co‑leadership was endorsed by two experts. Minor dissent existed regarding the differential diagnosis: Expert B initially excluded drug‑induced adrenal suppression, whereas Experts A and C later incorporated it after reviewing outlier input. Similarly, coagulopathy was highlighted as a potential additional concern by Experts A and C (and later accepted by Expert B) to guide work‑up for adrenal hemorrhage. All agreed that high‑dose IV hydrocortisone supplies adequate mineralocorticoid activity and that oral fludrocortisone should be restarted once the patient can tolerate PO.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Immediate bedside cardiac telemetry, invasive arterial blood pressure line, continuous pulse oximetry, urine output monitoring catheter, rapid bedside ultrasound of abdomen/adrenals if hemorrhage suspected, point‑of‑care glucose, arterial blood gas with lactate, repeat basic metabolic panel (electrolytes, BUN, creatinine), serum cortisol and ACTH if feasible, complete blood count, blood cultures, stool studies for bacterial superinfection, coagulation panel (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelets), and serum pregnancy test if applicable.  

Conclusion: Acute adrenal crisis secondary to missed glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement in a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate 1–2 L isotonic saline bolus followed by maintenance infusion; administer high‑dose IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 h (or continuous 200 mg/24 h) immediately; treat hyperkalemia with IV calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, and nebulized β‑agonist; give IV dextrose for hypoglycemia; start vasopressor (norepinephrine) if MAP remains <65 mmHg after fluids and steroids; provide anti‑emetic therapy (IV ondansetron 4–8 mg q8 h or metoclopramide 10 mg q6–8 h) to enable early return to oral steroids; obtain the diagnostic tests listed above, including coagulation studies to assess for coagulopathy and bedside ultrasound if adrenal hemorrhage is suspected; monitor continuously in ICU with cardiac telemetry, arterial line, hourly urine output, electrolytes/glucose/lactate every 2–4 h, and neurologic checks; once oral intake resumes, restart fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily; review current medications for CYP3A4 inducers or other agents that may increase steroid metabolism and adjust dosing accordingly; assess for concurrent infection and consider early broad‑spectrum antibiotics if bacterial sepsis is suspected; evaluate for other autoimmune endocrinopathies (thyroid antibodies, fasting glucose) and for pregnancy if applicable; arrange endocrinology follow‑up within 1–2 weeks, reinforce sick‑day rules, provide an emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone injection kit with written instructions, prescribe a medical‑alert bracelet, update vaccination status, and ensure primary‑care coordination.  

Notes: The patient’s lack of sick‑day education, emergency injection kit, and medical‑alert identification were key contributors to the crisis; these gaps must be corrected to prevent recurrence.

Age: 20 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the toes (interdigital) bilaterally for 2 weeks  

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) caused by dermatophytes, given the bilateral maceration, peeling, mild erythema, recent use of communal showers, and absence of systemic or severe local signs. All three experts agreed on this diagnosis and on the non‑emergent nature of the condition. Consensus also identified the need to recognize red‑flag features (pain, swelling, fever, extensive erythema, deep fissuring, purulent discharge, immunosuppression) that would require urgent evaluation. Where the panel differed, Experts A and B emphasized dermatology as the preferred specialty for definitive management, while Expert C highlighted that primary‑care clinicians can safely initiate treatment and that self‑care without a medical visit is reasonable for a mild, classic case. This divergence informs a stepwise approach: self‑care or primary‑care initiation is acceptable, with dermatology referral reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, treatment failure, or atypical presentations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for typical presentation. KOH microscopy or fungal culture may be performed only if the diagnosis is uncertain, the lesion is atypical, or there is failure to improve after an adequate trial of therapy.  

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis, uncomplicated, non‑emergent.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: The patient should apply a topical antifungal agent (e.g., terbinafine 1 % cream, clotrimazole 1 % cream, or miconazole 2 % cream) to the affected web spaces twice daily for 2–4 weeks, ensuring thorough coverage. Meticulous foot hygiene is essential: dry the feet completely after bathing, especially between the toes; wear flip‑flops or sandals in communal showers and pool areas; change socks at least daily; use an antifungal powder or spray inside shoes and consider treating footwear with an appropriate antifungal spray. The patient should avoid applying corticosteroid‑containing creams to the area, as this can mask infection and worsen tinea (tinea incognito). He may continue normal sports participation while using topical therapy, provided the medication does not cause skin irritation. He should monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection (increased pain, swelling, warmth, purulent discharge) and for any red‑flag features; if any develop, or if there is no improvement after 2 weeks of proper treatment, he should seek evaluation, preferably by a dermatologist. Because athletes are prone to recurrent exposure, counseling on environmental control and possible screening of close contacts (teammates, roommates) is advisable in outbreak settings. Adherence to the full treatment duration is critical to prevent recurrence, and follow‑up (in‑person or telehealth) after the treatment course can confirm resolution.  

Notes: No current indication for nail examination or systemic work‑up, as toenails are normal and the patient is immunocompetent.
